players.product: DataSafe TPPL (thin plate pure lead) UPS batteries and DataSafe Noir lithium battery systems for data centers, with installation and service

quarterly_data.signal: Data center business size and orders: CEO Sean put the data center business at about $400 million, and CFO Andi corrected that 'This year we'll round out to $500 million this year' (CEO: 'About $500 million this year for us'). CEO: EnerSys has 'a primary seat at the table with all of the hyperscalers' (not named) and also sells to the OEMs, the large uninterruptible power supply manufacturers. CFO: data center order rates were up in the mid-80s year over year in the first quarter; the lead-acid portion of the data center business had mid-teens year-over-year growth, and she expects it to be up high single to low double digits, sustainably, with the lithium product incremental share of wallet.
quarterly_data.figure: data center business about $500 million this year; Q1 data center order rates up in the mid-80s; lead-acid data center growth mid-teens

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sean on lead versus lithium in data centers: the Thin Plate Pure Lead battery, the same battery EnerSys deploys in U.S. nuclear submarines, drove the high double-digit order growth before the lithium product launched over the summer; lithium validations are going very well and demand is 'more of a pull from our customers than a push'. He expects lead-acid to keep growing — brownfield expansions are likely to stay like for like (fire suppression and architecture), and some municipalities are not ready for lithium so some greenfield sites still deploy TPPL — while the highest future growth rate is in lithium.

CEO Sean on cells and 800V: EnerSys is chemistry agnostic with a make-versus-buy strategy, sources cells all over the world with significant buying power, and adds its value after the cell (data-center form factor, a different battery management system, UPS communications interfaces, NFPA and UL requirements), so it is not subject to EV battery pricing. On 800V DC architectures, centralized UPS 'is not going anywhere'; higher voltage with batteries proximal to the load reduces the copper needed, and for EnerSys it is a change in form factor and voltage — an expansionary opportunity. He said one of the largest lithium suppliers into data centers before EnerSys entered offers customers a 72-hour email response, too slow when five nines of reliability allows 5 minutes of downtime a year.
quarterly_data.figure: competitor 72-hour response vs 5 minutes of allowed downtime a year

quarterly_data.signal: Network and broadband/utility: CEO Sean said EnerSys has over 50% market share in U.S. electric substations and is seeing double-digit growth in its substation business to support power demand; DOCSIS 4.0 is lifting the cable broadband business, and he said 80% of U.S. commercial industrial internet traffic goes over the Hybrid Fiber-Coaxial network that cable operators manage. CFO Andi: EnerSys has greater than 50% market share in almost all of the end markets it competes in.
quarterly_data.figure: over 50% U.S. electric substation share; 80% of U.S. commercial industrial internet traffic over HFC (CEO)

quarterly_data.signal: Aerospace and defense: CEO Sean said EnerSys is the largest battery supplier to the U.S. Department of Defense and many NATO allies (manned and unmanned systems, satellites, submarines, fighter aircraft, standoff weapons); its lithium silicon cobalt disulfide chemistry gives the most energy density for a joint standoff weapon, and stockpile replenishment is driving very robust backlog growth and accumulation; the Bren-Tronics acquisition took it deeper into soldier power, drone power and hybridized power at the forward edge of battle.

Greenville, South Carolina lithium cell plant: CEO Sean said that for 'that same gigawatt-ish of power' the plant will build something on the order of magnitude of 40 million cells, versus 8 to 9 million larger-format cells in the previous plan — two very high performance cells for defense programs, helping the Department of Defense consolidate some 42 soldier-power programs to under 9. CFO Andi: total capital investment conservatively around $650 million; the revised DOE award of $150 million is a cost share for equipment, not a loan, typically reimbursed with about a one-quarter lag; of about $200 million of state and local incentives, about a quarter to a third is short-term and the balance over the life of the plant. CFO: offtake is 'Not guaranteed', but the Department of Defense says it desperately needs this and is 'probably going to need bigger'; she expects additional capital expansion over and above the plant before it is operational. CEO: the 140-acre campus will also house a Lithium Center of Excellence and other parts of the PPS business.
quarterly_data.figure: about 40 million cells vs 8 to 9 million previously; total investment around $650 million; DOE award $150 million; about $200 million state and local incentives; 140 acres

quarterly_data.signal: Industrial mobility: CEO Sean said only about 67%, 68% of U.S. forklift fleets have been converted to electric, and flooded lead-acid is moving to maintenance-free (lithium and TPPL), which adds revenue and margin; forklift truck orders have 'finally started to see the nose up', with EnerSys battery orders lagging by about a quarter, and customers describe pent-up demand beginning to break free, though 'in sort of fits and starts'. Fuel cells remain under 1% or 2% of material-handling volume; EnerSys's monitoring has cut forklift fleet energy use by up to 30%, and it is pairing its BESS (Fortix) with forklift batteries at power-constrained sites.
quarterly_data.figure: about 67%, 68% of U.S. forklift fleets electric; fuel cells less than 1% or 2%; energy use cut up to 30%

quarterly_data.signal: Investor Day algorithm restated by CFO Andi: the end-market basket grows around 3%-5%, new products add an extra 1%-3%, for top-line growth of 4%-8%; margin expansion of 50-100 basis points per year; free cash flow conversion of about 80%-100%; by segment NIS around 4%-6%, IMS about 2%-4% and PPS 9%-11%, with NexSys, BESS and A&D the large contributors. She said this year starts mostly with margin expansion and revenue 'is really going to start to grow' toward the end of this year and into next.
quarterly_data.figure: top line 4%-8% (end markets 3%-5% plus new products 1%-3%); margin +50-100 basis points per year; FCF conversion 80%-100%; NIS 4%-6%, IMS 2%-4%, PPS 9%-11%

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Sean on M&A and positioning: EnerSys has 'a lot of dry powder', is 'actively in the market' and sees some 'really compelling' targets that would be quickly accretive and fill pieces of the power management equation; it is not in utility-scale storage (e.g. Fluence) or open C&I but works behind the meter, and he estimates EnerSys has about 80 to 90 gigawatts under management every day across its installed products.
quarterly_data.figure: about 80 to 90 gigawatts under management every day (CEO estimate)
